title: UHF RFID Hard Tags — Dual EAS + RFID for Retail Anti-Theft & Inventory Visibility
summary: In specification terms, UHF RFID hard tags combine Electronic Article Surveillance (EAS) anti-theft with item-level RFID inventory tracking in a single reusable tag. Attach at the source or in-store, deactivate at the POS, and reuse hundreds of times. The convergence of loss prevention and inventory visibility for apparel, footwear, accessories and specialty retail.
heroPoints: When the build spec is locked, dual EAS + RFID — one tag provides both anti-theft alarm at exit gates and item-level inventory data for EPC Gen2v2 / RAIN UHF readers.
Reusable design: detach at POS with a standard magnetic or mechanical detacher and reattach to new merchandise — 200+ qualified reuse cycles.
Compatible with Checkpoint EVOLVE, Sensormatic Synergy, Nedap !D Gate and Tyco ShrinkAlarm EAS gate systems alongside your existing RFID infrastructure.

sections.title: Problems retailers face when sourcing dual EAS + RFID hard tags
sections.intro: Converged hard tags touch three retail systems at once — EAS gate network, UHF RFID infrastructure and POS detach lanes. Sourcing missteps on any one of them surfaces only at live deployment, when rollback is expensive.
bullets: EAS frequency mismatch with existing gates. A retailer specifying RF 8.2 MHz hard tags receives AM 58 kHz tags instead; the tags pass silently through Checkpoint RF gates and trigger no alarm, with the error discovered only after live deployment.

Pin mechanism failure rate. Cheap pin tags fail the pin retention test at under 50 cycles, meaning staff cannot reattach them to new merchandise and must order replacements far more frequently than the 200-cycle specification suggests.

EPC data not set at source. Retailers expecting pre-encoded SGTIN-96 EPCs receive hard tags with blank EPC memory; the factory-side encoding step was not confirmed in the purchase order, and the buyer must encode 50,000 tags manually in-store.

Detacher compatibility: a retailer using Sensormatic Super Tag detachers discovers the new vendor's hard tags require a stronger neodymium detacher tool; this requires replacing detachers at every POS lane, an unbudgeted expense.

No source-tagging program for factory attachment. A brand wanting 100% tagging compliance from the factory cannot get its hard tag supplier to participate in a vendor-managed tagging program, forcing in-store attachment at higher labor cost.

sections.title: How Proud Tek solves EAS + RFID hard tag sourcing problems
sections.intro: Converged hard tags are a cross-domain product — they have to satisfy the loss-prevention team, the inventory-visibility team and the POS operations team simultaneously. sections.title: Operating notes drawn from converged EAS + RFID hard-tag programmes
sections.intro: Figures below are directional benchmarks drawn from buyer conversations and NRF / RILA / RAIN Alliance Retail Reference Implementation 2.1 playbooks; individual results depend on fleet size, EAS gate generation, source-tagging maturity and POS detach-lane design.
bullets: Retailers aligning EAS element frequency to gate infrastructure in the PO acknowledgement eliminate gate-silent batch failures — the single-largest cause of programme-level EAS rollback recorded in NRF ORC Survey responses.

Source-tagged converged hard tags collapse store-receiving labour relative to in-store tag-and-encode, because both the EAS element and the SGTIN-96 EPC are already live when the carton opens on the dock.

Converged EAS + RFID hard tags reduce per-item tagging spend versus parallel EAS + RFID labelling because one piece of hardware carries both duties over 200+ reuse cycles rather than one disposable RFID label per selling unit.

EPCIS 2.0 ObjectEvents from POS detach stations (bizStep='returning') paired with exit-gate EAS-trip exception events surface a clean shrinkage signal — unmatched EAS trips without a POS 'returning' event within 60 s — feeding Sensormatic Shrink Analyzer / Checkpoint HALO / Nedap iD Cloud analytics.

items.label: Weeks 1-2 — Gate & detach-lane audit
items.text: Confirm EAS gate make/model and frequency (RF 8.2 MHz vs AM 58 kHz) across every store; inventory current detacher tools at every POS lane and record their magnet/mechanical profile.

items.label: Weeks 3-4 — Tag spec lock & pre-encoding
items.text: Lock tag format (pin, lanyard, clamp, wrap, spider), chip family (Monza R6 / UCODE 8 / 9 / DNA / Higgs-9), EPC scheme (SGTIN-96 or SGTIN-198) against GS1 Company Prefix and item-reference master data.

items.label: Weeks 5-8 — Pilot store + source-tagging factory
items.text: Run one pilot store end-to-end (source-tagging factory → DC → back of house → sales floor → POS detach → reuse) and validate EPCIS 2.0 ObjectEvent flow into the loss-prevention analytics layer.

items.label: Month 3+ — Chain scale-out & recirculation loop
items.text: Scale source-tagging to all participating factories; establish the detached-tag collection + re-shipment-to-factory loop; tune alarm-suppression rules in Sensormatic Synergy / Checkpoint EVOLVE for the 60 s POS-deactivation window.

sections.title: EAS + RFID convergence
sections.intro: Traditionally, retailers needed separate EAS tags (for anti-theft) and RFID tags (for inventory). Converged hard tags combine both functions into a single device.

sections.title: Tag formats
bullets: Pin tag (pencil tag). Attaches through fabric with a steel pin. Standard for apparel, most common format.
Lanyard tag: loops through zipper pulls, shoe eyelets, handbag hardware. No piercing required.
Clamp tag: grips the edge of flat-packed goods like bedding, towels, boxed items.
Wrap tag: secures around bottle necks, wine bottles, small electronics packaging.
Spider wrap: adjustable cable wrap for irregularly shaped merchandise.

sections.title: Deployment
bullets: Source tagging: attach hard tags at the factory or distribution center for 100% tagging compliance from day one.
In-store tagging: attach at the sales floor using magnetic or mechanical pin tools.
POS deactivation: the EAS function is deactivated during checkout; the RFID chip remains readable for returns processing.
Detaching: use standard magnetic or mechanical detachers (compatible with existing Checkpoint/Sensormatic tooling).
Recirculation: collect detached tags at POS and reattach to new merchandise.

sections.title: RFID data capabilities
bullets: EPC memory: 96-128 bits — encode SGTIN-96 for item-level identification matching your barcode database, or SGTIN-198 for luxury alphanumeric serials.
User memory: 32-512 bits (chip-dependent). Store supplementary data like price zone, season code or vendor ID.
EAS bit: set/clear the EAS flag for gate alarm activation/deactivation.
Kill/access passwords: protect against unauthorized modification or decommissioning.

faq.question: Are these compatible with our existing Checkpoint gates?
faq.answer: Yes. Our hard tags are available with RF 8.2 MHz EAS elements compatible with Checkpoint systems, or AM 58 kHz elements compatible with Sensormatic systems. Specify your gate manufacturer and we match the EAS frequency. The UHF RFID component is standard EPC Gen2v2 (ISO/IEC 18000-63:2015) and works with any RAIN Alliance Endorsed reader.

faq.question: How many times can a hard tag be reused?
faq.answer: Our hard tags are designed for 200+ attach/detach cycles. The mechanical pin mechanism and EAS/RFID electronics maintain full functionality throughout the tag's service life. Tags should be retired when the pin mechanism shows wear or the housing is visibly damaged. Pin-retention sampling to 200 cycles is executed per batch during QC.

faq.question: Can hard tags be source-tagged at the factory?
faq.answer: Yes. Source tagging hard tags at the factory or DC ensures 100% tagging compliance, reduces in-store labor and enables RFID inventory visibility from the moment goods arrive. We can pre-encode the EPC with your SGTIN-96 or SGTIN-198 data and set the EAS bit during manufacturing.

faq.question: How does the converged EAS + RFID hard tag integrate with loss-prevention analytics and GS1 EPCIS 2.0 inventory visibility?
faq.answer: The EAS element triggers the gate alarm on Checkpoint EVOLVE / Sensormatic Synergy / Nedap iSense / Tyco ShrinkAlarm gates via the existing RF 8.2 MHz or AM 58 kHz field; the same tag emits an EPC Gen2v2 response captured by overhead or gate-mounted UHF readers (Impinj R700, Zebra FX9600, Nedap !D Cloud). The UHF ObjectEvent is emitted per EPCIS 2.0 (ISO/IEC 19987:2015) with bizStep='departing' at the exit gate and bizStep='returning' at the POS detach station — feeding Sensormatic Shrink Analyzer, Checkpoint HALO, Zebra SmartLens for Retail, Nedap iD Cloud and Sensormatic IQ. For brand-side analytics (Sellbytel, Detego, Impinj ItemSense) the same EPCIS stream flows via REST. Each deployment's EAS + RFID fusion rules (alarm suppression within 60 s of POS deactivation, exception flagging for EAS-tripped EPCs absent from POS transactions) are documented in the integration run-book shipped with every order.

faq.question: Which retail anti-theft standards, ORC regulations and EAS certifications govern hard tag acceptance?
faq.answer: EAS elements meet EN 50357 (AM 58 kHz) / EN 50364 (RF 8.2 MHz) electromagnetic-field exposure limits and ICNIRP 2020 guidelines. Metal Detector / EAS Coexistence is tested per EN 300 330 (SRD at 9 kHz–30 MHz) and FCC Part 15 Subpart B. Organized Retail Crime (ORC) programmes — NRF ORC Survey, RILA ORC Council, Project Boost, InterORC — reference RF or AM EAS as primary loss-prevention control plus item-level RFID as exception-analytics layer; the 2024 U.S. INFORM Consumers Act (15 U.S.C. §45f) and the EU Digital Services Act Article 31 (high-risk goods online sales) accept RFID serial history as primary evidence for marketplace seller verification. Converged hard tags align to the NRF Point-of-Sale Data Standards v10 for return-authorization, and the RAIN Alliance Retail Reference Implementation 2.1 for retailer RFID deployments.
